note: One tag = one wrong idea. Reuse before creating. Each tag needs 3+ questions across the platform, 2+ of them hidden recap variants (pool: recap).

tags.label: Thinks water is absorbed somewhere other than the large intestine
tags.fix: Water is absorbed from the undigested food in the large intestine. What is left becomes faeces.

tags.label: Mixes up what the mouth, gullet and stomach each do
tags.fix: Mouth: teeth cut and grind the food, and saliva mixes in. Gullet: muscles squeeze the food down to the stomach; no digestive juice is made there. Stomach: muscles churn the food while gastric juice digests it into a thick liquid.

tags.label: Thinks digested food is absorbed somewhere other than the small intestine
tags.fix: Digestion is completed in the small intestine, and the digested food passes through its wall into the blood.

tags.label: Thinks digestion is finished in the stomach
tags.fix: The stomach only partly digests the food. Digestion is completed in the small intestine.

tags.label: Gets the order of the digestive parts wrong
tags.fix: Food moves one way only: mouth → gullet → stomach → small intestine → large intestine.

tags.label: Mixes up what happens to digested and undigested food
tags.fix: Digested food passes into the blood in the small intestine. Undigested food, such as fibre, cannot pass into the blood: it moves on to the large intestine, where water is absorbed from it, and leaves the body as faeces.

tags.label: Mixes up the jobs of the body systems
tags.fix: Respiratory: takes in oxygen and removes carbon dioxide. Circulatory: carries digested food, water and oxygen to all parts of the body. Digestive: breaks food down. Skeletal: supports, shapes and protects. Muscular: works with the skeleton to move body parts.

tags.label: Puts a body part in the wrong system
tags.fix: Nose, windpipe, lungs: respiratory. Heart, blood, blood vessels: circulatory. Mouth to large intestine: digestive. Bones: skeletal. Muscles: muscular.

tags.label: Doesn't know what digestion is for
tags.fix: Digestion breaks food down into simpler substances that are small enough to pass into the blood. Carrying them around the body is the circulatory system's job.

tags.label: Thinks digestion begins somewhere after the mouth
tags.fix: Digestion begins in the mouth. The teeth cut and grind the food, and saliva, a digestive juice, starts to digest it.

tags.label: The moving thing carries a force
tags.fix: A moving object carries a force inside it, given by whatever set it moving.

tags.label: It stops when its force runs out
tags.fix: A moving object stops because its force runs out, not because a force such as friction acts on it.

tags.label: Still things have no forces on them
tags.fix: An object that is not moving has no forces acting on it.

tags.label: Gravity only works sometimes
tags.fix: Gravity acts only at certain times: only when falling, not when resting, held, moving up, near a magnet or on the Moon.

tags.label: Friction is always bad
tags.fix: Friction is always unwanted and should be removed.

tags.label: Smooth means no friction
tags.fix: Smooth surfaces have no friction.

tags.label: Friction pushes things along
tags.fix: Friction acts in the direction of motion and helps objects move.

tags.label: Springs stretch the same every time
tags.fix: How much a spring stretches does not depend on the load.

tags.label: Length and extension are the same
tags.fix: The length of a spring and its extension are the same thing.

tags.label: A spring doesn't push back
tags.fix: A stretched or squashed spring pushes or pulls the same way it is being moved, or not at all.

tags.label: Change everything at once
tags.fix: In an experiment, several variables can be changed at once, or the variable being tested is kept the same.

tags.label: Double the load, double the length
tags.fix: Doubling the load doubles the length of the spring, rather than its extension.

tags.label: A force needs touching
tags.fix: A force can act only when two things touch.

tags.label: Forces only start things moving
tags.fix: A force can only start things moving. It cannot stop, slow, turn or change the shape of an object.

tags.label: Magnets act on everything
tags.fix: A magnet affects every object, or every metal.

tags.label: Magnets only push
tags.fix: Attraction and repulsion are mixed up: a magnet pushes away objects it attracts.

tags.label: Gravity only acts on big things
tags.fix: Only large objects experience gravitational force.

tags.label: Names an effect the force did not have
tags.fix: Any effect of a force will do, instead of the one that matches what actually changed.

tags.label: Blames gravity for every change
tags.fix: Gravitational force is given as the reason for a sideways or backwards change, when gravity pulls only towards the Earth.

tags.label: Reads one step of the table as the total
tags.fix: The change for one step in a results table is taken as the total change, without counting the steps.

tags.label: Thinks gravitational force pushes
tags.fix: Gravitational force is described as a push away from the Earth rather than a pull towards it.

tags.label: Thinks heat and temperature are the same thing
tags.fix: Temperature is how hot something is. Heat is energy. More water at the same temperature holds more heat; the same water at a higher temperature holds more heat.

tags.label: Thinks "cold" is something that flows or is given out
tags.fix: Only heat flows, always from hotter to colder. Something feels or becomes cold because it loses heat.

tags.label: Thinks heat flow stops before, or goes past, the point where both temperatures are equal
tags.fix: Heat flows from hotter to colder until both reach the same temperature, somewhere in between, and then it stops.

tags.label: Mixes up heat gain and heat loss when a temperature changes
tags.fix: If the temperature rises, the object gained heat. If the temperature falls, it lost heat.

tags.label: Thinks mass changes when something expands or contracts
tags.fix: Expanding or contracting changes the volume, not the mass.

tags.label: Mixes up when things expand and when they contract
tags.fix: Gaining heat makes things expand. Losing heat makes them contract. Solids, liquids and gases all do this.

tags.label: Mixes up good and poor conductors of heat
tags.fix: Metals are good conductors: heat flows through them easily. Wood, plastics, air and rubber are poor conductors. Metal feels cold because it conducts heat away from your hand fast.

tags.label: Misreads a thermometer, or trusts touch to measure temperature
tags.fix: Find what one small mark is worth, then count from the nearest number below. Touch only tells you how fast heat leaves your hand, so use a thermometer.

tags.label: Mixes up heat gain and heat loss in a change of state
tags.fix: Melting, boiling and evaporating need heat gain. Freezing and condensing happen through heat loss.

tags.label: Mixes up what is and is not a source of heat
tags.fix: A source of heat produces heat: the Sun, burning things, switched-on appliances, rubbing things together. Ice, the Moon and switched-off appliances produce none.

tags.label: Exhaled air has no oxygen
tags.fix: We use up all the oxygen, so the air we breathe out has none left.

tags.label: Gas exchange happens in the nose or windpipe
tags.fix: Oxygen enters the blood in the nose, windpipe or blood vessels rather than the lungs.

tags.label: The parts do each other's jobs
tags.fix: The jobs of the nose, windpipe and heart are mixed up (for example the windpipe filters the air).

tags.label: The heart is part of breathing
tags.fix: The heart takes in oxygen, pumps air or does gas exchange, so it belongs to the respiratory system.

tags.label: The lungs use up the oxygen
tags.fix: Oxygen is used in the lungs, not at the body cells.

tags.label: Air in and air out are the same, or all oxygen in and all carbon dioxide out
tags.fix: The change in gases between breathed-in and breathed-out air is mixed up.

tags.label: Blood only carries oxygen
tags.fix: Blood carries only one thing, or is not changed when it passes through the lungs.

tags.label: Blood vessels carry air
tags.fix: Air, not blood, travels in the blood vessels, or the heart is a tube.

tags.label: Every animal breathes with lungs
tags.fix: Fish, plants or other living things take in oxygen the way humans do.

tags.label: Plants do not use oxygen
tags.fix: Only animals take in oxygen and give out carbon dioxide.

tags.label: Plants have no tubes
tags.fix: Plants do not carry water and food inside them.

tags.label: Gets the order of the air path wrong
tags.fix: The parts of the respiratory system are put in the wrong order, or the breathing-out path is given for breathing in.

tags.label: Thinks blood vessels pump the blood
tags.fix: The pumping job of the heart is given to the blood vessels.

tags.label: Thinks the cells store the oxygen
tags.fix: Oxygen delivered to the body cells is stored rather than used to release energy from food.

tags.label: Picks the wrong part of a fish
tags.fix: A part used for swimming or feeding is chosen as the part that takes in oxygen from the water.

tags.label: Mixes up which animals have 3-stage and which have 4-stage life cycles
tags.fix: 4 stages (egg, larva, pupa, adult): butterfly, beetle, mosquito. 3 stages: cockroach and grasshopper (egg, nymph, adult), and chicken and frog (egg, young, adult).

tags.label: Mixes up what a larva, a pupa and a nymph are like
tags.fix: Larva: unlike the adult; eats a lot. Pupa: unlike the adult; does not feed or move while the adult forms inside. Nymph: like the adult but smaller and wingless.

tags.label: Gets the order of the stages wrong
tags.fix: 4 stages: egg → larva → pupa → adult. 3 stages: egg → nymph (or young) → adult. A plant: seed → young plant → adult plant → seed.

tags.label: Thinks a life cycle ends at the adult
tags.fix: The adult reproduces (it lays eggs, or makes seeds), so the stages start again. That is why it is a cycle.

tags.label: Mixes up the stages of a plant's life cycle
tags.fix: Seed → young plant (roots, stem, leaves, no flowers) → adult plant (flowers, then fruits with seeds) → seed. The seeds come from the adult plant's fruits.

tags.label: Thinks all living things have the same life cycle
tags.fix: Different living things have different life cycles: different stages, and different lengths of time.

tags.label: Thinks a young animal that looks different is a different kind of animal
tags.fix: A tadpole is a young frog, and a caterpillar is a young butterfly. They look different from their adults but grow into them.

tags.label: Thinks walking away from a lamp makes your shadow on the ground shorter
tags.fix: With a lamp above you shining down on the ground, the farther you are from the lamp, the more the light slants and the longer your shadow. Right under the lamp, the shadow is only a small patch at your feet.

tags.label: Thinks a shadow can point towards the light, or follows the way you face
tags.fix: Light travels in straight lines from the light source. The shadow forms where the object blocks the light, so it is always on the side of the object away from the light.

tags.label: Thinks light can bend around an object, or that a shadow is a reflection
tags.fix: Light travels in straight lines, so it cannot bend around an object. A shadow is the area the light cannot reach because the object blocks it.

tags.label: Thinks moving an object closer to a torch makes its shadow on a screen smaller
tags.fix: Between a torch and a screen, the closer the object is to the torch, the more light it blocks, so the bigger its shadow on the screen.

tags.label: Thinks only the size of the object decides the size of its shadow
tags.fix: The size of the object matters, but so do the distances between the light, the object and the screen or ground. Move any of them and the shadow changes.

tags.label: Changes the wrong thing, or more than one thing, in a shadow investigation
tags.fix: Change only the variable being tested. Keep the object, the light and every other distance the same, so any change in the shadow comes from that one variable.

tags.label: Mixes up which objects are light sources and which only reflect light
tags.fix: A source of light gives off its own light: the Sun, a lit candle, a firefly. The Moon, mirrors and shiny objects only reflect light from a source.

tags.label: Mixes up how we see objects (light from the eyes, or only light sources can be seen)
tags.fix: We see an object when light from it enters our eyes. A source gives off its own light; any other object is seen when it reflects light from a source into our eyes.

tags.label: Thinks a material that lets light through makes no shadow, or an equally dark one
tags.fix: An object that lets no light through makes a dark shadow. One that lets some light through makes a lighter shadow. One that lets most light through makes almost no shadow.

tags.label: Thinks a shadow keeps the same shape whichever way the object faces
tags.fix: A shadow has the outline of the object as seen from the light. Turn the object and the shadow's shape can change: a round plate seen edge-on makes a thin bar.

tags.label: Thinks moving the screen further from the object makes the shadow smaller
tags.fix: With the torch and the object still, the further the screen is from the object, the bigger the shadow.

tags.label: Thinks something is living because it moves, makes sounds or gets bigger
tags.fix: A living thing needs water, food and air, grows, responds and reproduces: all of these. A car moves and a balloon gets bigger, but neither is living.

tags.label: Thinks plants or seeds are not living, or that plants don't need air or food
tags.fix: Plants are living. They need water, air and food (they make their own), grow, respond and reproduce. A seed is living: it grows when it gets water.

tags.label: Mixes up which characteristic of living things an example shows
tags.fix: Getting bigger: grows. Reacting to a change (touch, light): responds. Making young: reproduces. Dying without water, food or air: needs them to survive.

tags.label: Groups an animal by where it lives or how it moves, not by its body features
tags.fix: Look at body features. A bat flies but has fur: a mammal. A penguin can't fly but has feathers: a bird. A sea turtle lives in the sea but has dry, scaly skin: a reptile.

tags.label: Mixes up the body features of the animal groups
tags.fix: Fur or hair: mammal. Feathers and a beak: bird. Scales and fins: fish. Moist, smooth skin: amphibian. Dry, scaly skin: reptile. 6 legs and 3 body parts: insect (a spider, with 8 legs, is not one).

tags.label: Thinks fungi are plants
tags.fix: Fungi (mould, mushrooms, yeast) are not plants: they are not green and cannot make their own food.

tags.label: Thinks bacteria can be seen with the eyes alone, or are not living
tags.fix: Bacteria are living things too small to see without a microscope. They are found everywhere, even where we can't see them.

tags.label: Thinks every plant has flowers, or that a plant without flowers is not a plant
tags.fix: Non-flowering plants, such as ferns and mosses, never make flowers, but they are still plants.

tags.label: Groups living things by a feature the chart or table does not use
tags.fix: Read the chart's question, or the table's headings, and use only that feature. Size, colour and favourite places don't count unless the chart asks about them.

tags.label: Picks advice without checking what fungi like
tags.fix: Fungi grow where it is warm, dark and damp and there is food. Good advice takes at least one of these away. If a choice changes none of them, it will not help.

tags.label: Thinks covering or closing things keeps fungi out
tags.fix: A closed shoe, bag or cupboard keeps things warm, dark and damp. That helps fungi grow. Open, airy and dry places are better.

tags.label: Thinks dead skin or dirt is harmless, not food for fungi
tags.fix: Fungi feed on dead things such as dead skin, dirt and old bread. Take the food away and they grow less.

tags.label: Forgets that fungi need water, and keeps things damp
tags.fix: Fungi need water. Wet shoes, damp cloths, steam and sweat help them grow. Keeping things dry slows them down.

tags.label: Picks a place with only one thing fungi like
tags.fix: Fungi grow fastest where all four things are there: warmth, darkness, water and food. One thing on its own, such as warmth or darkness, is not enough.

tags.label: Thinks iron or steel can repel
tags.fix: Only a magnet can push another object away. If two objects repel, both of them are magnets.

tags.label: Thinks iron and steel blocks pull each other
tags.fix: Iron and steel are magnetic materials, not magnets. Two plain iron or steel blocks show no force on each other; they are only pulled by a magnet.

tags.label: Forgets that a magnet attracts every iron or steel block
tags.fix: A magnet attracts every iron or steel block placed beside it. If a magnet shows no force with an object, that object is not iron or steel.

tags.label: Thinks a magnet can push or pull plastic or wood
tags.fix: Plastic and wood are non-magnetic. A magnet shows no force at all with them.

tags.label: Thinks attracting means one object must be a plain iron or steel block
tags.fix: Two magnets attract too, when unlike poles face each other. Attract only tells you that at least one of the pair is a magnet.

tags.label: Thinks two magnets can show no force on each other
tags.fix: Two magnets placed beside each other always push or pull. No force means at least one of the pair is not a magnet.

tags.label: Thinks a compass always points north, even with a magnet close by
tags.fix: A compass needle is a small magnet that can turn freely. It rests pointing North–South only when no magnet is near. A magnet close by pushes and pulls its poles and decides which way it points.

tags.label: Mixes up which poles attract and which repel
tags.fix: Unlike poles attract (N and S). Like poles repel (N and N, or S and S). So a needle's N end is pulled towards a S pole and pushed away from a N pole.

tags.label: Forgets that a freely suspended magnet comes to rest with its N pole pointing north
tags.fix: A magnet that can turn freely, with no other magnet near, swings and then comes to rest pointing North–South, with its N pole towards the north.

tags.label: Thinks a magnet must touch something to push or pull it
tags.fix: A magnet can push or pull without touching. A compass needle turns, and paper clips jump up, while the magnet is still some distance away.

tags.label: Thinks a magnet can have only one pole, or no pole at one end
tags.fix: Every magnet has two poles, one N and one S, at its two ends. If you know one end, the other end is the opposite pole.

tags.label: Thinks a magnet attracts or repels every metal
tags.fix: A magnet acts only on magnetic materials: at P3, iron and steel. It neither attracts nor repels other metals, such as aluminium and copper.

tags.label: Mixes up how to make a magnet by stroking, or what can be made into one
tags.fix: Stroke an iron or steel object many times, in the same direction, with the same pole. Only iron and steel can be made into magnets: aluminium, copper and plastic cannot.

tags.label: Mixes up what makes an electromagnet stronger, or what to change when testing it
tags.fix: More coils of wire, or more batteries, make an electromagnet stronger. To test one of these, change only that one and keep the other the same.

tags.label: Thinks a magnet is strongest in the middle, or equally strong all along
tags.fix: A magnet is strongest at its poles, near its two ends. Most paper clips cling to the ends.

tags.label: Thinks an object resting on another shows a magnetic force
tags.fix: An object resting on a stand shows nothing about magnets: any solid stand holds an object up against gravity. Only a push — the object floating away — shows a magnetic force at work.

tags.label: Uses "strong" to explain a bending job
tags.fix: Strong means it can take a load without breaking. Flexible means it can bend without breaking. Shaping, folding and wrapping are all bending, so they need a flexible material.

tags.label: Picks a property the job never uses
tags.fix: First ask what is being done to the material: is it bent, loaded, wetted, floated or lit? Only the properties that job uses can be the answer, even if the other statements are true.

tags.label: Treats one property as proof of another
tags.fix: Each property has its own test. Passing the bend test tells you nothing about the load test, and floating tells you nothing about soaking up water.

tags.label: Checks only one of the properties the job needs
tags.fix: List every property the job needs first, then check each material against the whole list. A material that fails even one property on the list is not suitable.

tags.label: Mixes up what to change, keep the same and measure in a fair test
tags.fix: In a fair test only the type of material is changed. Everything else that could affect the result, such as size, amount of water, time or how far it is bent, is kept the same. The result is what you measure.

tags.label: Forgets that a part which bends must be flexible
tags.fix: Any part that folds, wraps or moves with you has to bend without breaking. A material with no tick for flexible would crack there.

tags.label: Forgets that a part which meets water must be waterproof
tags.fix: Rain, wet floors and the water inside a container all mean the same thing: that part must not absorb water.

tags.label: Compares the masses instead of working out the water absorbed
tags.fix: The masses include the material itself, so the biggest mass is usually just the heaviest material. Water absorbed = mass after soaking − mass before soaking. Work it out for every material, then compare.

tags.label: Mixes up waterproof and absorbent
tags.fix: Waterproof means the material does not absorb water, so its mass does not change when it is soaked. A towel must do the opposite: absorb as much water as possible.

tags.label: Judges by how big the jump looks, not the grams of water absorbed
tags.fix: The pieces are the same size, so compare the grams of water each one absorbed. A jump that looks big on a light piece can still be fewer grams than a smaller-looking jump on a heavy piece.

tags.label: Mixes up how much light a material lets through
tags.fix: Clear glass, clear plastic and food wrap let most light through. Frosted glass and tracing paper let some through. Wood, metal and rubber let none through.

tags.label: Thinks big or heavy things sink and small or light things float
tags.fix: Whether an object floats depends on what it is made of. A large wooden log floats; a small steel nail sinks.

tags.label: Gets the properties of one of the seven materials wrong
tags.fix: Wood and metal are strong. Rubber and fabric are flexible. Glass and ceramic are not flexible: they break when bent. Plastic, rubber and glass are waterproof; fabric is absorbent. Cork, Styrofoam and most wood float; metal, glass, clay and rock sink.

tags.label: Thinks air is not matter, so an "empty" container has nothing in it
tags.fix: Air is matter: it has mass and takes up space. A bottle that looks empty is full of air, and that air takes up the space inside it.

tags.label: Thinks air can be squashed until it takes up no space
tags.fix: Air can be compressed into less space, but it always takes up some space. The more it is squashed, the harder it pushes back.

tags.label: Thinks air has no mass
tags.fix: Air is matter, so it has mass. Pumping more air into a ball makes its mass slightly greater.

tags.label: Mixes up the shape and volume of solids, liquids and gases
tags.fix: A solid has a definite shape and a definite volume. A liquid has a definite volume but takes the shape of its container. A gas has no definite shape or volume: it fills its whole container and can be compressed.

tags.label: Gives another reason when it is trapped air that is pushing back
tags.fix: When something cannot get into a closed container, check for air already inside. The trapped air takes up space and, with no way out, it pushes back.

tags.label: Thinks light, heat, sound or a shadow is matter
tags.fix: Matter has mass and takes up space. Light, heat and sound are forms of energy: they have no mass and take up no space, so they are not matter.

tags.label: Thinks powders like sand or sugar are liquids because they can be poured
tags.fix: Each grain keeps its own definite shape and volume, so a powder is a solid. The heap only takes the container's shape because the grains slide past one another.

tags.label: Reads the final water level as the volume of the object
tags.fix: The level after includes the water. Volume of the object = level after − level before, or the volume of water that overflows.

tags.label: Mixes up mass and volume
tags.fix: Mass is measured on a balance, in g or kg. Volume is the space taken up, in mL or cm³. A bigger object is not always the heavier one.

tags.label: Thinks a plant takes in food from the soil, or that a part other than the leaves makes food
tags.fix: The leaves make the plant's food. The roots take in water and mineral salts from the soil, and mineral salts are not food.

tags.label: Thinks a part other than the roots takes in water from the soil
tags.fix: The roots take in water and mineral salts from the soil. The stem only carries the water up, and the leaves don't take it in.

tags.label: Mixes up which part holds the plant in the ground and which holds it upright, or why
tags.fix: The roots hold the plant firmly in the ground. The stem holds the plant upright and supports its leaves, so they get as much sunlight as possible.

tags.label: Thinks the stem carries only water, or carries things only one way
tags.fix: The stem carries water and mineral salts up from the roots, and food from the leaves to all the other parts, including down to the roots.

tags.label: Thinks damage to one part affects only that part
tags.fix: The parts work together. Without roots, no water reaches the leaves. Without leaves, no food is made for the rest of the plant. Parts above a broken stem get no water.

tags.label: Doesn't recognise a leaf, stem or root when it looks different
tags.fix: Look at where the part is and what it does. A tree's trunk is its stem. A tiny seedling already has leaves, a stem and roots.

tags.label: Picks the wrong apparatus to observe or measure plant parts
tags.fix: A hand lens makes small parts look bigger. A ruler measures length. A measuring cylinder measures volume, a balance measures mass and a thermometer measures temperature.

tags.label: Uses one bar, or adds the wrong bars, to find how long it takes to reach a stage
tags.fix: Each bar shows the days spent in ONE stage. To find how long it takes to reach a stage, add the bars of the stages before it, in order. Do not add the stage you are reaching, or the stages after it.

tags.label: Names a stage or an animal that the graph or table does not give
tags.fix: Use only what the graph or table shows. Egg, young and adult are stages; they do not say that the young stage is a nymph, or which animal it is.

tags.label: Puts a day in the wrong stage by not adding the earlier stages first
tags.fix: Stages follow one after the other. To find the stage on a given day, add the bars one by one until you pass that day.

tags.label: Explains with what a container lacks (such as no Substance X) instead of what fungi need
tags.fix: Say what fungi need, and which container has it. Mould needs water and warmth. Substance X takes in water, so the pear next to it is dry. "It has no Substance X" does not say what the mould needs.

tags.label: Compares containers that differ in more than one thing, or in the wrong thing
tags.fix: To test one factor, change only that factor and keep everything else the same. To test water, compare two containers at the same temperature that differ only in water.

tags.label: Thinks a magnet cannot lose its magnetism
tags.fix: A magnet can lose some of its magnetism. Dropping it many times, hitting it hard or heating it makes it weaker. (This is not in the syllabus LO list, but it is tested in school papers.)
